title: The athlete's heart: bigger chambers, slower beats
goal: Explain how endurance training enlarges the heart, how fast it happens, how to read heart-size data fairly, and why a bigger stroke volume lowers resting heart rate and raises maximal cardiac output.

steps.title: Volume load, pressure load
steps.text:
The heart grows to fit the work it is given, and the kind of work shapes how it grows.

- **Volume load.** Hours of running or riding send large volumes of blood back to the heart. The chamber gets bigger and the wall thickens in proportion: [eccentric hypertrophy](g:eccentric-hypertrophy).
- **Pressure load.** Heavy lifting raises blood pressure in short bursts. The wall thickens without a bigger cavity: [concentric hypertrophy](g:concentric-hypertrophy).

A meta-analysis of 59 [echocardiography](g:echocardiography) studies (1451 male athletes) tested this split. Relative wall thickness (wall thickness vs cavity size) was 0.36 in controls, 0.39 in endurance athletes and 0.44 in strength athletes; endurance athletes' cavity only tended to be wider than strength athletes' (53.7 vs 52.1 mm) [[c:heart-pluim]].

claims.text: Endurance and strength athletes showed divergent cardiac adaptations, with relative wall thickness 0.36 in controls, 0.39 in endurance and 0.44 in strength athletes.

evidence.quote: The overall mean relative left ventricular wall thickness of control subjects (0.36 mm) was significantly smaller than that of endurance-trained athletes (0.39 mm, P=0.001), combined endurance- and strength-trained athletes (0.40 mm, P=0.001), or strength-trained athletes (0.44 mm, P<0.001).
showed a trend toward a difference with respect to posterior wall thickness (10.3 versus 11.0 mm, P=0.078) and left ventricular internal diameter (53.7 versus 52.1 mm, P=0.055)
Results of this meta-analysis regarding athlete's heart confirm the hypothesis of divergent cardiac adaptations in dynamic and static sports.

steps.title: A newer look: volume, method and body size
steps.text:
A later meta-analysis of elite young male athletes refined the picture [[c:heart-utomi]]:

| | endurance | resistance |
|---|---|---|
| left ventricle end-diastolic volume | 171 mL | 131 mL |
| clear concentric pattern? | – | not found |

So the bigger *volume* of the endurance heart is the robust finding; the thick-walled 'strength heart' was not.

Two cautions for reading any of these numbers:

- **Method.** [Cardiac MRI](g:cardiac-mri) gave larger volumes than echocardiography: 178 vs 135 mL.
- **Body size.** Bigger people have bigger hearts; [left ventricular mass](g:lv-mass) rose with body surface area.

Compare hearts only measured the same way and scaled for size.

claims.text: In elite male athletes, LV end-diastolic volume was larger in endurance than resistance athletes (171 vs 131 mL); a concentric pattern was not found in resistance athletes; MRI gave larger volumes than echocardiography; body size predicted heart mass.

evidence.quote: Only LV end-diastolic diameter and volume were higher in endurance athletes than in resistance athletes: 54.8 mm (95% CI 54.1 to 55.6) vs 52.4 mm (95% CI 51.2 to 53.6); p<0.001 and 171 ml (95% CI 157 to 185) vs 131 ml (95% CI 120 to 142); p<0.001, respectively.
A training-specific pattern of concentric hypertrophy was not discerned in resistance athletes. Both imaging mode and BSA can have a significant impact on the interpretation of AH data.
LV end-diastolic volume was larger when CMR was used rather than echocardiography: 178 ml (95% CI Q7 162 to 194) vs 135 ml (95% CI 128 to 142); p<0.001.
Meta-analysis regression models demonstrated positive and significant associations between body surface area (BSA) and LV mass, RV mass and LA diameter.

steps.title: One year from couch to marathon
steps.text:
Cross-sectional comparisons can't separate training from talent. So 12 sedentary adults (7 men, 5 women) trained for a year to run a marathon, with heart MRI every 3 months [[c:heart-arbab]]:

- VO₂max rose from 40.3 to 48.7 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹, with bigger maximal stroke volume and cardiac output.
- Left and right ventricular mass grew to levels seen in elite athletes.
- The **right** ventricle enlarged from the start. The **left** first thickened (concentric), and only after 6–9 months did its cavity widen, restoring the usual shape [[c:heart-arbab-sequence]].
- Its stretchiness (compliance) still fell short of elite hearts.

So a year builds the size; the elite heart's full filling capacity may take longer, or need talent.

claims.text: One year of intensive endurance training in sedentary adults raised VO₂max from 40.3 to 48.7 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹ and ventricular mass to elite levels, without reaching elite compliance.

evidence.quote: Mean max rose from 40.3±1.6 to 48.7±2.5 mL/kg per minute after 1 year (P<0.00001), associated with an increase in both maximal cardiac output and stroke volume.

One year of prolonged and intensive endurance training leads to cardiac morphological adaptations in previously sedentary young subjects similar to those observed in elite endurance athletes; however, it is not sufficient to achieve similar levels of cardiac compliance and performance.

claims.text: The left ventricle first remodelled concentrically for 6–9 months, then dilated; the right ventricle remodelled eccentrically from the outset.

evidence.quote: Contrary to conventional thinking, the left ventricle responds to exercise with initial concentric but not eccentric remodeling during the first 6 to 9 months after commencement of endurance training depending on the duration and intensity of exercise. Thereafter, the left ventricle dilates and restores the baseline mass-to-volume ratio.

steps.title: A bigger stroke, a slower beat
steps.text:
What does a bigger left ventricle buy? A bigger [stroke volume](g:stroke-volume). Since **cardiac output = HR × SV**:

- **At rest**, the body needs about the same 5 L·min⁻¹ as before. With more blood per beat, fewer beats do it: hence the slow resting heart rate of the [athlete's heart](g:athletes-heart). (The heart-rate module covers the nerve and pacemaker side of [sinus bradycardia](g:sinus-bradycardia).)
- **At maximum**, HRmax barely changes with training, so the bigger SV goes straight into a bigger maximal cardiac output: the main reason VO₂max rises.

Pumping function at rest is normal: [ejection fraction](g:ejection-fraction) didn't differ between athletes and controls [[c:heart-normal]]. When athlete's heart overlaps with disease is a medical question, covered in the module *The athlete's heart, AF and sudden cardiac death*.

claims.text: Athletes' hearts showed no difference from controls in ejection fraction and other measures of pumping and filling function.

evidence.quote: With respect to cardiac function, there were no significant differences between athletes and control subjects in left ventricular ejection fraction, fractional shortening, and E/A ratio.

steps.title: Same output, fewer beats
steps.problem: At rest a cyclist needs a cardiac output of 5.6 L·min⁻¹. Before training her stroke volume is 80 mL; after years of training it is 100 mL. What resting heart rate does each need?
steps: HR = cardiac output ÷ SV. Convert to the same unit: 5.6 L·min⁻¹ = 5,600 mL·min⁻¹.
After: 5,600 ÷ 100 = 56 beats·min⁻¹. Same output, 14 fewer beats a minute.

points: Endurance training is a volume load: the left ventricle grows by eccentric hypertrophy (bigger cavity, matching wall).
The bigger endurance chamber (171 vs 131 mL in one meta-analysis) is the solid finding; a thick-walled 'strength heart' is less clear.
Compare hearts only by the same method (MRI reads larger than echo) and scaled for body size.
In one year sedentary adults reached elite ventricular mass; the left ventricle thickened first and widened after 6–9 months; elite compliance wasn't reached.
Bigger SV gives the same resting output with fewer beats, and more maximal output at the same HRmax; pumping function stays normal.

variants.stem: Why does endurance training mainly enlarge the heart's chamber, rather than just thicken its wall?

options.text: Hours of high blood return load it with volume
options.why: Right: a volume load stretches the chamber, which grows with a matching wall: eccentric hypertrophy.

options.text: Endurance training raises blood pressure more than lifting
options.why: Brief, very high pressures come from heavy lifting, which favours wall thickening.

options.text: The heart muscle shrinks to make room for more blood
options.why: The wall thickens a little too; the heart grows overall.

options.text: Higher heart rates stretch the wall thinner
options.why: Faster beating shortens filling; the chamber grows from volume load, not rate.

variants.stem: Cycling and rowing mix long volume loads with high-force strokes. Given the meta-analysis values for endurance (0.39) and strength athletes (0.44), where would you expect these combined-sport athletes to fall for relative wall thickness?

options.text: Between the two groups; the meta-analysis found 0.40
options.why: Right: a mix of both loads gave a value in between, 0.40.

options.text: Above strength athletes, because rowing is so hard
options.why: They were at 0.40, below strength athletes' 0.44.

options.text: Below untrained controls, because the cavity grows most
options.why: Controls had the lowest value, 0.36.

options.text: Equal to controls, since the two loads cancel
options.why: 0.40 was clearly above controls' 0.36.

variants.stem: Study A (echocardiography) reports runners' left ventricle volume as 140 mL; study B (cardiac MRI) reports 175 mL in a similar group. What is the best conclusion?

options.text: The gap may be mostly method: MRI reads larger volumes than echo
options.why: Right: in pooled data MRI gave 178 vs 135 mL for echo. Compare like with like.

options.text: Group B trained far more and has much bigger hearts
options.why: Method alone can explain a gap this size; you can't credit training.

options.text: Study A is wrong, as echocardiography doesn't measure volume
options.why: Echo does measure volume, just systematically lower than MRI.

options.text: Group B has heart disease
options.why: A larger MRI volume in athletes is expected and says nothing about disease here.

variants.stem: A 95 kg, 1.95 m rower has a heavier left ventricle than a 58 kg, 1.68 m triathlete. What must you do before concluding his heart adapted more?

options.text: Scale for body size, such as body surface area
options.why: Right: heart mass rises with body surface area, so raw values favour big athletes.

options.text: Nothing: heavier heart means more adaptation
options.why: Bigger bodies have bigger hearts regardless of training.

options.text: Compare their maximal heart rates
options.why: HRmax doesn't tell you how much the heart grew.

options.text: Check that both were measured with echocardiography only
options.why: Same method matters, but it doesn't remove the body-size effect.

variants.stem: In the year-long marathon study, how did the left ventricle first respond to training?

options.text: Its wall thickened first; its cavity widened only after 6–9 months
options.why: Right: initial concentric remodelling, then dilation.

options.text: Its cavity widened from the first month
options.why: That was the right ventricle; the left lagged.

options.text: It didn't change in the first year
options.why: Its mass reached elite levels.

options.text: It shrank as the right ventricle took over
options.why: Both ventricles grew.

variants.stem: The one-year study followed 12 sedentary adults with no control group. What does that design limit?

options.text: How general and how certain the size of the changes is
options.why: Right: 12 people, no comparison group, so the exact numbers are rough, though the direction is clear.

options.text: Whether training rather than talent can enlarge a heart
options.why: That is what the longitudinal design does answer: the same people changed with training.

options.text: Whether MRI can measure ventricular mass
options.why: MRI is the more exact method; that is not the limit.

options.text: Whether VO₂max rose
options.why: VO₂max rose from 40.3 to 48.7 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹, a large, clear change.

variants.stem: A runner needs a resting cardiac output of 5.4 L·min⁻¹. His stroke volume rises from 75 mL to 90 mL with training. What is his resting heart rate after training?

options.text: 60 beats·min⁻¹
72 beats·min⁻¹
options.why: That is the before value (5,400 ÷ 75).

options.text: 0.06 beats·min⁻¹
options.why: This forgets to convert L to mL: 5.4 ÷ 90.

options.text: 486 beats·min⁻¹
options.why: This multiplies: 5.4 × 90. HR = output ÷ SV.

variants.solution: HR = cardiac output ÷ SV = 5,400 mL·min⁻¹ ÷ 90 mL = 60 beats·min⁻¹ (before: 5,400 ÷ 75 = 72).

variants.stem: A triathlete needs a resting cardiac output of 6.0 L·min⁻¹. Her stroke volume rises from 80 mL to 120 mL over years of training. What is her resting heart rate after?

options.text: 50 beats·min⁻¹
75 beats·min⁻¹
options.why: That is the before value (6,000 ÷ 80).

options.text: 0.05 beats·min⁻¹
options.why: This forgets to convert L to mL: 6.0 ÷ 120.

options.text: 720 beats·min⁻¹
options.why: This multiplies: 6.0 × 120. HR = output ÷ SV.

variants.solution: HR = cardiac output ÷ SV = 6,000 mL·min⁻¹ ÷ 120 mL = 50 beats·min⁻¹ (before: 6,000 ÷ 80 = 75).

variants.stem: A cyclist needs 5.2 L·min⁻¹ at rest. His stroke volume rises from 65 mL to 104 mL. What is his resting heart rate after?

options.text: 50 beats·min⁻¹
80 beats·min⁻¹
options.why: That is the before value (5,200 ÷ 65).

options.text: 0.05 beats·min⁻¹
options.why: This forgets to convert L to mL: 5.2 ÷ 104.

options.text: 541 beats·min⁻¹
options.why: This multiplies: 5.2 × 104. HR = output ÷ SV.

variants.solution: HR = cardiac output ÷ SV = 5,200 mL·min⁻¹ ÷ 104 mL = 50 beats·min⁻¹ (before: 5,200 ÷ 65 = 80).

variants.stem: A runner's HRmax stays at 190 beats·min⁻¹ while training raises her maximal stroke volume from 110 to 130 mL. By how much does her maximal cardiac output rise?

options.text: 20 L·min⁻¹
options.why: 20 is the SV change in mL; multiply it by HR and convert: 190 × 20 mL = 3.8 L·min⁻¹.

options.text: 0 L·min⁻¹, since HRmax didn't change
options.why: Cardiac output is HR × SV; a bigger SV raises it even at the same HR.

options.text: 3,800 L·min⁻¹
options.why: This forgets to convert mL to L.

variants.solution: Q = HR × SV. Before: 190 × 110 mL = 20,900 mL·min⁻¹ = 20.9 L·min⁻¹. After: 190 × 130 = 24,700 mL·min⁻¹ = 24.7 L·min⁻¹. Rise: 3.8 L·min⁻¹.

variants.stem: A cyclist's HRmax stays at 180 beats·min⁻¹ while his maximal stroke volume rises from 120 to 150 mL. By how much does his maximal cardiac output rise?

options.text: 30 L·min⁻¹
options.why: 30 is the SV change in mL; multiply by HR and convert: 180 × 30 mL = 5.4 L·min⁻¹.

options.text: 0 L·min⁻¹, since HRmax didn't change
options.why: A bigger SV raises Q even at the same HR.

options.text: 5,400 L·min⁻¹
options.why: This forgets to convert mL to L.

variants.solution: Q = HR × SV. Before: 180 × 120 mL = 21.6 L·min⁻¹. After: 180 × 150 mL = 27.0 L·min⁻¹. Rise: 5.4 L·min⁻¹.

variants.stem: Compared with untrained people, what is the resting ejection fraction of an endurance athlete's heart, typically?

options.text: About the same: pumping function is normal
options.why: Right: the meta-analysis found no difference in ejection fraction.

options.text: Much higher, which is why stroke volume is bigger
options.why: SV is bigger mainly because the chamber holds more, not because a bigger share is ejected.

options.text: Much lower, a sign of a weakened heart
options.why: Athletes' hearts showed normal function.

options.text: Zero at rest, since the heart rate is so slow
options.why: Every beat ejects blood; a slow rate doesn't stop ejection.
